Senses.Explanation: A formal teaching-hall address or observance, conventionally headed “ascend the hall” (上堂). The term occurs 54,942 times in 402 allowlisted texts and is the principal public format in recorded sayings. The corpus treats it as a completed event and as an institution requested by officials or imperial command, scheduled in the monastic code, announced by a placard, delegated to a head monk holding the whisk, or formally suspended and later resumed. Addresses open with speech after a pause, a raised old case (上堂舉), or a monk’s public question (上堂僧問); headings also specify occasions such as entering a monastery or release from the restriction period. Chan turns an ordinary ascent phrase into the standard name of the abbot’s public teaching-hall address and its recorded discourse.
Senses.Note: Primary Zen-institutional sense. Split from the concrete act of ascending or taking the seat. Contrast the “small convocation” (小參), an informal convocation with no fixed place. The added delegated-whisk and prohibited/resumed witnesses establish institutional authority and control, not more occasion headings.

Senses.Explanation: The concrete institutional action: ascend the teaching hall or take its high seat. Linji’s record pairs the request that he “take the seat” (升座) with “the master ascended the hall” (師上堂). The resulting address is a different thing and belongs to the primary sense.
Senses.Note: The paired “take the seat” construction (升座) is the clearest non-heading anchor for the physical action.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, honored or venerable, and senior or long-established. The compound occurs 1,906 times in 291 allowlisted texts and serves as a title for an established Chan elder. Biographies say that someone traveled to consult venerable elders; records speak collectively of venerable elders in every region, elder predecessors, and old venerable elders. It also appears in the title 'Recorded Sayings of the Ancient Venerable Elders.' In Huangbo's reported exchange, a monk objects that venerable elders everywhere gather communities and teach people after Huangbo says there are no Chan teachers; Huangbo replies that he did not say there was no Chan, only that there were no teachers. A portrait verse can use 'one of this sort is called a venerable elder' satirically, showing that the title can be quoted rather than simply bestowed by the narrator.
Senses.Note: The corpus provides no stable graph-formula definition of the bare title. The four strings ending in 'venerable elder is ...' are relative-clause constructions, not definitions. Productive modifiers include 'in every region' (71 hits in 55 texts), 'old' (22 in 19), and 'elder predecessors' (10 in eight).
